OMEGA Intelligence is a separate product from CREED. It uses no CREED rules and no SMC rules: trend, structure, momentum, volatility, range position, volume, novelty and cross-market relationships are all computed by its own engine. It shares the Journal and the Brain with CREED, but each writes under its own name and neither reads the other’s signals. Right now it describes markets; it does not issue trade signals. Leverage — what the tests say

Leverage multiplies losses exactly as much as gains, and no tested rule has an edge large enough to lever. CREED: −0.10R to −0.12R a trade after costs (E29, E31); at 1% risk it loses half the account within a year in 76% of 100,000 simulated accounts. The panic bounce H1 run as a 100 USDT account of 5–10 USDT seats without leverage still fell 56–59% from its peak (E26). The default here (5% margin × 10×) puts half the account into every position; at 10× a 9% move against you liquidates it before most stops. OMEGA Prime’s tickets use 1× isolated and the Bridge caps a Binance order at 10 USDT. Use these pages to see the damage on paper, not to pick a higher setting.

🌱 Growth & Discipline

Your real edge in dollars, how fast it compounds at a sustainable pace, and the discipline habits that keep you in the game long enough to grow.

Log at least 5 trades to unlock your growth analytics.
Every trade you log — win or loss — teaches the app your real edge. This page turns that history into honest numbers about where you stand and what to work on.

💵 Your Real Edge (Expectancy)

Expectancy = the average amount you win or lose per trade, measured from your own logged history. This is the single most important number in trading. If it's positive, you make money over time. If it's negative, no position size or discipline will save you — the strategy itself needs work.

📈 Sustainable Growth Projection

Based on your real expectancy and a fixed-fractional risk model (risking the same % each trade). This is how disciplined accounts actually compound — slowly, then powerfully. Change the inputs to see honest timelines.

⚠ Risk of Ruin

The probability that a losing streak wipes out a big chunk of your account before your edge plays out. This is the number that kills amateur accounts. Lower risk-per-trade dramatically lowers this.

🎯 Discipline Score

Trading success is 20% strategy, 80% behaviour. This scores the habits that separate profitable traders from the rest — measured from patterns in your logged trades.

1

Check your state

Trading failure is mostly behavioral. Before markets, check yourself honestly.

2

Read the regime

What market are you in? Run analysis on your instrument and note the regime. You don't trade every market — some regimes have no edge.

Run an analysis; the detected regime will appear here.
3

Scan for a setup

Look for a qualifying signal. If there's no clean setup, that's a valid and common outcome — the discipline is to wait.

No setup? Good. Doing nothing is a position. Most of a professional's day is waiting. Come back later or tomorrow — there's no prize for forcing trades.
4

Size it correctly

Risk a small, fixed % of your account (1% is a solid default). Use the position-size calculator on the Signals page so the loss to your stop equals exactly that %.

5

Pre-trade gate

The final checklist before you commit. Every box must be checked — if any fails, skip the trade.

Check all boxes to unlock.
6

Execute & log

Take the trade exactly as planned. Don't move your stop. When it closes, log it honestly — including whether you followed your plan.

After the trade closes, log it as a Win/Loss and answer the plan-adherence questions. That adherence data is what turns your Discipline score real.
7

Review

End the session with a look at your real numbers. Over time this is where you learn whether your edge is real.

WhatsApp signal

How this works, honestly: a web page cannot silently send WhatsApp messages — that needs a server holding a WhatsApp API token, and a token embedded in a file like this one would be readable by anyone who opened it. What this does instead is build the signal and open WhatsApp with it pre-filled, so sending is one tap. Would the Brain take this?

Run CREED to get a second opinion.

The Brain scores setups from your journal history. It does not gate CREED — it gives an opinion, and where it disagrees with the method that disagreement is shown rather than hidden.

Signals being tracked — taken or not

No signals tracked yet.

This is what keeps the sample honest. If only the trades you happened to be awake for were recorded, the record would measure your availability as much as the strategy. Every confirmed setup is followed to its stop or target and written to the journal as creed-signal with taken: false — separable from trades you actually placed, and never counted as real.

Are the gates earning their place?

Every setup a gate turns down is followed to its outcome as if you had taken it. If rejected setups would mostly have lost, the gate is protecting you; if they would mostly have won, it is costing you winners. Rejections go into the journal as creed-rejected with the gate and reason, and are kept out of the Brain’s trade statistics — a rejected setup losing is evidence the gate worked, not a losing trade.

Before you read any of these numbers

Hypothetical performance disclosure (CFTC Rule 4.41). Backtested and simulated results have inherent limitations. Unlike a real record, simulated results do not represent actual trading and no money was risked. They are prepared with the benefit of hindsight, and no representation is made that any account will or is likely to achieve profits or losses similar to those shown.

Everything on this page marked simulated is hypothetical. Only rows marked live came from a trade you actually took. The two are never mixed in any statistic here — but the difference matters far more than any number on the page.

This is not financial advice. It is a research tool you are building for yourself. It does not know your circumstances, is not a registered adviser or broker, places no orders, and can be wrong. Market data may be delayed, incomplete, or wrong. Trading carries a real risk of losing money, and leveraged instruments can lose more than you put in.

Your journal lives only in this browser. Export a backup regularly.

Your acceptance ruleYours, not the course's

The course shows acceptance on charts but never defines it numerically — it never says how many closes must hold, or whether a wick counts. This is your definition. Keep it fixed and let the journal tell you whether it holds up; changing it mid-sample destroys the record.

"Sweep must exceed by" auto-scales to whatever instrument is loaded — a sensible starting point for gold, forex or crypto, refined against the real price after your first run. Type your own value here and it stops adjusting for you.

Three settings that exist only to stop the engine calling something a trade when it probably isn’t — none of these are in the course, they’re here so the mechanical rules can’t fool themselves: Scan window is how far back it looks for a sweep, not just the latest few hours. Min. reward:risk throws out anything that doesn’t offer real reward relative to its risk — a thin one is usually noise. Max. reward:risk catches the opposite problem: an absurdly high ratio is a symptom, not a prize. It happens when the swept level is small and sits mid-range (usually the 1H pullback zone), so the stop is tiny while the target is still the far side of the whole battlefield — a 54:1 setup is really asking price to travel a quarter of its own value in one trade. The course’s own worked examples run 4.85–9.71:1, because there the sweep sits at a battlefield edge so stop and target are at opposite ends. Over the ceiling you can either reject the setup (default) or tick trim target, which keeps the trade but pulls the target in to exactly your ceiling — realistic, but a deliberate deviation from the course’s “target the opposite objective” rule. Min. structure compares the battlefield’s height to the instrument’s ordinary bar-to-bar range — a “battlefield” barely wider than typical noise isn’t a real one. Every event found is still listed below in Recent Setups, even the ones these two reject, so nothing is hidden — only kept out of the live verdict.

Session filter is off by default and is not from the course either — it comes from general market-structure research: gold specifically trades with the tightest spreads and clearest moves during the London/New York overlap (~13:00–17:00 UTC); outside it, spreads widen and moves get noisier, which is a plausible reason a mechanical scan can flag something a discretionary trader watching only that window would never have considered. Turn it on to restrict the live verdict to those hours — events outside the window still appear in Recent Setups, just excluded from being picked.

The sequence

  1. 4H — direction and arena. Mark swing highs and lows. The two extremes are the liquidity objectives; the range between them is the battlefield. Structure gives the primary trend, which is the only direction you may trade.
  2. 1H — the move in progress. Find the leg happening now inside the primary trend and mark the pullback zone.
  3. 15M — the sweep. Wait for price to reach a liquidity objective or the pullback zone and push through it, taking the stops resting there.
  4. 15M — acceptance. Price must settle back on the other side and hold. Sweep alone is not a signal. Sweep that keeps going is a real break. Sweep plus acceptance is the trade.

What this page does not know

Acceptance is not defined numerically by the course. The threshold above is yours. Every “setup confirmed” verdict depends on it, so treat it as a hypothesis you are testing rather than a rule you were handed.
The pullback zone is drawn by hand in the course. This page proposes one from the most recent 1H consolidation. Check it each session and override when it is wrong.
Every example in the source material is bar replay — moves that had already happened. Replay cannot tell you whether you can call a sweep in advance. Only forward records can, which is what the journal is for.

Price ladder

The battlefield drawn to scale. Objectives are the boundaries; the shaded band is the pullback zone.

Runs checks against the real functions in this file, on this device. The point is that you can confirm the build you have open is correct yourself, rather than taking a test count on trust.

Load the file a tester sent you — their Journal → Export CSV, or a full backup. Browsers cap this kind of storage at roughly 5 MB. Past that, saves start failing — usually silently, which is how a journal quietly stops recording. Back up before pruning: the export above captures every key in this browser, not just trades.

About this page

Prices are Swissquote’s live bid and ask, read by your OMEGA Live API every few seconds. Spread is ask minus bid, in pips (0.0001; 0.01 for yen and forint pairs); for metals it is in dollars. When a quote is more than ten minutes old the market is closed (weekends, holidays) or the feed paused, and the row says so.

Candles for the chart come from Twelve Data when this browser has a key; without one they come from the Live API (Twelve Data on the server if it has a key, otherwise Yahoo: 1 hour back 2 years, 15 minutes back 60 days, 5 minutes back 5 days). Metal candles from Yahoo are futures (gold GC, silver SI, platinum PL, palladium PA): a close proxy, not spot. The chart says which source it used.

The board needs the Live API token (Settings › Data & Keys). Information only: OMEGA places no orders, and forex majors failed every hour-by-hour test OMEGA ran (E15).

About

OMEGA, explained

Everything OMEGA does, where its data comes from, and what the evidence says. Open any section.

What OMEGA is

OMEGA is a trading companion that runs in your browser. It reads crypto, forex and metals markets, shows them clearly, tests ideas with fair rules before trusting them, and runs paper bots so a rule can prove itself on live prices first.

It places no real orders. Nothing in this app is connected to a broker. Your data stays on this device unless you download a backup.

Its standing rules: never invent data; plan a test before looking at the data and count every try; paper first; no secrets in files or backups.

Signals, grades and the evidence behind them

Every test was planned and fingerprinted before its data and run once; results are after trading costs.

Grade A Climax reversal

A 3σ hourly drop on 3× normal volume that closes in the top 40% of its range: buy the next open, hold 12 hours. It passed on 324 untouched coins. Over all perpetuals in 2025–26 it still averaged +109 bp a trade, but not significantly (t 0.78), so its forward record decides.

Grade B Panic bounce (H1 and H3)

Buying coins that fell far below their own normal range. Plan E22: H1 +0.36% a trade (t 4.34), H3 +0.22% (t 3.63). E25, with 143 delisted coins included (883 coins): H1 +0.32% (t 4.54), H3 +0.30% (t 4.08).

It lives on the big rebounds: without the best 5% of trades each version loses about 0.7% a trade, and single trades lost 77–93%. Run as a 100 USDT account (E26) it had drawdowns of 56% and 59%. In 2025–26 its edge was +18 bp a trade (t 0.59): positive, not significant.

Grade C Watch list and the Daily Plan

Ideas that failed their final test but stay on paper to be watched: the panic bounce on 5- and 15-minute bars (E37 +31.8 bp, t 1.05; E38 +2.8 bp, t 0.10), the market-wide 15-minute panic (E40 +24.7 bp, t 0.74) and the UpScout top-2% longs (E81). Without their best 5% of trades E37 and E40 lose (−32.7 and −44.1 bp). They are never real trades. The Daily Plan is grade C too: a written plan per coin, followed on paper, not a tested edge.

CREED: measured as a coin flip

After a CREED setup, price behaves like a fair coin: it reached +1R before the stop 49% of the time against 50% for chance. Per trade after costs: −0.118R, −0.100R and −0.118R on three coin sets (about 11,000 setups). Longs-only, BTC-context, panic-gated and volatility-buffer versions all failed on untouched coins (E29, E31). In 100,000 simulated accounts, CREED at 1% risk lost half the account within a year in 76% of them. Treat a CREED “Ready” as structure, not a promise.

What failed

Daily-trading rules (12,480 tried, E28), order-book depth and crowd positioning (E30), a neural network (E32), funding harvest (E34: +8.8% a year in 2021–24, −17% a year in 2025–26), forex majors hour by hour (E15), trend, momentum and funding rules (E50–E55), new data sources (E63–E70) and exit tweaks (E80: the original exits were best). The lesson: size is predictable, direction is not; panic selling gets overdone.

The bots

In-app bots (Bots page): the OMEGA bot, CREED bots 1 and 2, the Confluence bot and the Portfolio bot, and the Growth Bot on the Risk Guard page. All trade on paper against real prices and run only while the app is open.

24/7 cloud bots: a paper bot runs every hour on GitHub and trades only the approved rules (A, B, and the C watch list on paper). Its positions, resting orders and recent actions are published on the bot-state branch. The laptop Station runs the same bot and scouts when the laptop is on; the Live API reads the Station when it runs next to it, otherwise the cloud record.

Scouts: UpScout and DownScout forecast a big move in the next 24 hours from hourly candles (E81), the fast scouts the next 4 hours from 15-minute candles (E82). They see big moves coming but failed as trading rules, so they are scored forward against the base rate and feed no bot.

Everything the bots show is paper or forecast information, never an order.

The Live API and your token

The OMEGA Live API is a small read-only server (default https://omega-live-api.onrender.com) that gathers forex quotes and candles, crypto data and the bots feed. It never places orders and holds no exchange keys.

Its address and your token live in Settings › Data & Keys. The token is kept on this device only, like an API key: it is never written into a backup and a backup file can never set it. Health, the pair list and the Academy are public; prices, candles and the bots feed need the token. A server that has slept takes about a minute to wake.

The Academy

A course on markets, chart reading, risk first and testing an idea before trusting it, with quizzes and progress kept on this device. Modules 1 and 2 and the first lesson of every module are free and also built into the app for offline reading; the rest unlocks with a license key. The tutorial can be reopened from the Academy or Settings.

Risk and leverage

The Risk Guard rules: 0.5% of the account a trade, at most 2 open, stop trading after −2% in a day or −5% in a week.

Measured leverage on the short-timeframe panic trades (E37, E38, E40; 5% margin a trade): at 1× no liquidations (drawdown 10–15%); 2× already liquidates; at 20× 29–31% of trades hit the liquidation distance and the account goes to about 1 USDT; 40× liquidates about 60% of trades. The worst move inside one bar was −83% (October 2025).

No strategy tested turned 100 into 1,000,000 in 5 simulated years. Trading carries a high risk of losing money; leverage can lose the whole deposit quickly.

Privacy and backups

Everything (journal, settings, progress) is stored in this browser. Nothing leaves it except the requests for market data, the Live API and the Academy, and what you set up yourself (alerts, the Claude council with your own key).

A backup file leaves out every API key and token, the alert webhook and your WhatsApp number; restoring a file can never set them. Re-enter keys after restoring on a new device. The app only runs scripts from itself and its chart library (Content-Security-Policy).

The progress board

Research ideas, tests, verdicts and the live bots’ records are published on the progress board: omega-board.onrender.com.

Diagnostics — self-test, storage, errors
Educational research tool. Structure, liquidity, regime, and risk-sizing figures are computed with documented rule-based and statistical methods on real market data — not a trained predictive model. Probability bands reflect a Bayesian update of your own logged track record (wide and uninformative until you've logged real outcomes), not a guarantee. Sentiment and narrative text are LLM interpretations of headlines, not verified facts. Always apply independent risk management.
